boxes.title: NoteFrom my experience: an urge at the toilet door
boxes.text: NoteFrom my experience: an urge at the toilet door I sometimes notice this when I approach a toilet: a need that did not feel pressing moments earlier suddenly does. The setting has changed much faster than the bladder could have filled. A familiar opportunity to act may direct attention toward the sensation and activate a learned association between that place and urination.

boxes.title: NoteFrom my experience: my daughter learning to count
boxes.text: NoteFrom my experience: my daughter learning to count Figure 8.3: Counting on fingers makes an arithmetic procedure visible. With suitable practice and feedback, the answer may later be retrieved without counting. In Figure 8.3, my three-year-old daughter uses her fingers as an external counting tool to compute 4 + 1. She had to hold the problem in mind, map numbers onto fingers, and inspect the result. The same answer later can arrive without visible counting. With suitable practice and feedback, some components of an initially effortful, rule-guided activity can become faster and more automatic.

boxes.title: NoteFrom my experience: a fall becomes a somersault
boxes.text: NoteFrom my experience: a fall becomes a somersault My daughter once fell from a small toddler chair. I first checked that she was not seriously hurt and acknowledged the pain she might genuinely be feeling. I then exclaimed, “Wow, you did a somersault like a kung fu master!” She laughed proudly instead of crying. Describing the fall as an impressive performance offered a less threatening interpretation, which may have changed her emotional response. Safety and validation must come first. A calm, reassuring frame can sometimes reduce fear, but it should never deny injury, dismiss pain, or require another person to feel differently.

boxes.title: NoteFrom my experience: leaving the amusement park
boxes.text: NoteFrom my experience: leaving the amusement park When it is time to leave an amusement park, I have learned to ask my daughter, “Do you want to leave now or in five minutes?” If I ask only, “Do you want to leave now?”, she usually says no: she wants to keep playing. With the second question, she almost always chooses “In five minutes.” Sometimes she even reminds me that the five minutes are up and we should leave. The question shifts the decision from whether to leave to when to leave. Compared with demanding an immediate departure, it gives her a small part of the decision to make herself. My impression is that this makes leaving feel more like carrying out her own plan. The five minutes also give her time to prepare for the transition. The choice works as a shared agreement when I can genuinely accept either answer and honor the extra time. Leaving is the boundary; the timing is hers to choose.

boxes.title: NoteFrom my experience: a holiday that became €300 more expensive
boxes.text: NoteFrom my experience: a holiday that became €300 more expensive Once, my wife and I found a good deal for a holiday: €3,000 for one week at an all-inclusive resort. We were excited about it. When we returned the next day to book, the price had risen by €300, to €3,300. We still considered it a good deal and booked the trip, but paying the additional €300 felt bad. The original €3,000 quote had become our reference point. We were evaluating the holiday against both the alternatives available to us and the price we had expected to pay. Against the first comparison, the trip remained attractive; against the second, the extra €300 felt like a loss. The price increase was a real additional cost, but the earlier quote also gave that cost a particular meaning: we were losing a deal we had already begun to anticipate. A purchase can therefore remain worth making while feeling disappointing relative to an expectation.

boxes.title: NoteFrom my experience: replacing cola with sparkling water
boxes.text: NoteFrom my experience: replacing cola with sparkling water I like cola, including zero-sugar cola, but I want to drink it less often. The thought of having some often arrives when I feel a little drowsy or eat a heavy meal. If cola is within easy reach, I can find myself pouring a glass before giving the choice much thought. Access makes a difference. At home, when cola is not readily available, the urge can pass without my acting on it. Replacing it with sparkling water has also worked well for me: I still have something fizzy to drink, and I find that the urge for cola subsides. This gives the familiar cue another action to lead to, while making the old action less convenient. I could also use drowsiness as a prompt to begin a small exercise habit: “When I feel drowsy at home, I will do one push-up.” But the setting matters. One push-up is a small physical task, yet doing it in a restaurant would feel awkward. There, ordering sparkling water is a much easier response. A replacement needs to fit the place in which the cue occurs, as well as the behavior I want to change.

boxes.title: NoteFrom my experience: one egg or two?
boxes.text: NoteFrom my experience: one egg or two? At breakfast, I might ask my daughter, “Would you like one egg or two?” rather than “Do you want eggs?” The question gives her a choice about quantity, but it also assumes that she wants an egg. If eggs are optional, “no egg” needs to remain an easy, respected answer. A small choice supports agency when it leaves room for what she actually wants.
